background: In September 2026, Swiss medical device company Medela was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign . The data allegedly obtained in the breach was later published publicly and included 424k unique email addresses belonging predominantly to healthcare professionals, Medela staff and leads. The exposed data consisted primarily of corporate contact information, including names, physical addresses and phone numbers, with some records also containing associated support tickets.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In September 2026, Swiss medical device company Medela was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign .
outcome: 423,947 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Salutations, Support tickets.
editorial: The distinction in this record is between professional contact information and an assumption about medical records. Have I Been Pwned's description says the addresses belonged predominantly to healthcare professionals, staff and leads. Its listed fields include employers, job titles and support tickets. That does not establish that patient histories or clinical records were exposed, and this entry should not be read as making that additional claim.

Support-ticket context can make a fraudulent follow-up more convincing than a generic message. A sender may mention a product, workplace or earlier enquiry and ask the recipient to open an attachment or change payment instructions. This is a plausible risk from the listed fields, not evidence that such a campaign has been observed in this incident.

Verify an unexpected request using a contact route you already know rather than the number or link inside the message. For an organization, the useful response is to identify which business addresses and support interactions are affected, inform the appropriate internal security contact, and preserve suspicious messages through the normal reporting process. Do not circulate the leaked dataset to colleagues to look for their names.

A breach entry does not establish that your current account is compromised or that the affected service has reset its access controls. The source describes an extortion campaign and publication of allegedly obtained data. It does not document the exact intrusion path. Keep that unknown separate from the published contact-data description; guessing an unpatched system or stolen credential would add a causal story the available record does not support.

background: In August 2026, healthcare and pharmaceutical company McKesson was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign . The group subsequently published a substantial corpus of data they alleged was sourced from the company, which included 6.4M unique email addresses among other personal and corporate data attributes. The impacted data related to a range of individuals and roles, including marketing campaign recipients, patients, staff and healthcare provider contacts.

In McKesson's disclosure notice , the company advised it had identified unauthorised access to "certain third-party applications and the exfiltration of certain data was associated with a subset of customers within our Oncology & Multispecialty and Medical-Surgical business units", but had "reasonable assurance of no ongoing unauthorized activity".
how: In McKesson's disclosure notice , the company advised it had identified unauthorised access to "certain third-party applications and the exfiltration of certain data was associated with a subset of customers within our Oncology & Multispecialty and Medical-Surgical business units", but had "reasonable assurance of no ongoing unauthorized activity".
motive: In August 2026, healthcare and pharmaceutical company McKesson was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign .
outcome: 6,404,340 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Employers, Genders, Names, Personal health data, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Read the data classes rather than the headline. "Personal health data" sitting next to names, dates of birth, employers and addresses is the combination that makes a breach at a distributor behave like a breach at a hospital, and McKesson is a wholesaler, not a care provider. Most of the people in this file have never knowingly had a relationship with it.

That is the pattern worth internalising about healthcare supply chains. The companies holding your health data are rarely the ones you chose: they are the clearing houses, distributors, benefit administrators and billing intermediaries that sit behind the clinic. You cannot audit them, opt out of them, or in most cases name them. The practical consequence is narrow and specific.

Health-adjacent detail is what makes a fraudulent call convincing, a caller who knows your employer, your date of birth and something about your medication has not proved they are your pharmacy. Treat any unexpected contact referencing your care as unverified, and go back through a number you already had.

background: In August 2026, clothing retailer Carhartt was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign . The group subsequently published data allegedly obtained from the company including 12.9M unique email addresses, names, phone numbers and physical addresses. The published corpus also contained millions of synthetic records that did not relate to real individuals and were excluded from the breach.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In August 2026, clothing retailer Carhartt was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign .
outcome: 12,933,413 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: The published corpus contained millions of synthetic records, fabricated rows matching no real person, which were identified and excluded before the figure of 12.9 million was settled on. That detail is worth more than the breach itself, because the number an extortion crew posts and the number of people actually in the file are routinely different numbers, and the first one is the one that becomes the headline. Padding pays twice.

A larger file sells for more, and a company forced to answer for an inflated figure looks worse than it is, which is useful leverage when the demand is "pay or we publish". Establishing what is actually in a dump is slow, unglamorous work, and a breach story that leads with the raw row count is a story where nobody has done it yet.

What genuinely leaked here is ordinary: name, email address, phone number, home address. No passwords, no card numbers, nothing that opens an account. That combination does not get into anything, it gets a convincing message about a delivery problem on an order you could plausibly have placed. The uptick in parcel texts after a retail breach is not a coincidence, and it is the whole return on data like this.

background: In August 2026, millions of records allegedly sourced from Chess.com were posted online . The data contained 7.3M rows with 4.6M unique email addresses, along with usernames, names, countries and data relating to users' Chess.com accounts. Analysis of the data suggested it had been obtained by scraping. editorial: Two details in this record deserve more weight than the total. The first is that analysis indicated the data was scraped rather than taken from a database, collected through interfaces that were working as designed, at a scale nobody intended. The second is that 99% of the addresses had already appeared in earlier breaches. Both facts cut the same way, and not in the direction most people assume.

A scrape means no password was exposed, so there is nothing to reset. A 99% overlap with previous incidents means almost nobody in this file is newly exposed. If you are in it, this is very unlikely to be the breach that matters to you, one of the earlier ones already was. What it does add is linkage.

A username joined to a real name, a country and a confirmed email address is exactly the material used to connect a pseudonymous account to a person. If your chess handle is one you also use elsewhere, that connection is now easier for anyone to make, and no password change undoes it.

editorial: Read the disclosure language and the outcome side by side. The company described "a limited set of data from a webpage hosted by Salesforce on its platform". More than 100GB was subsequently published, carrying 13.5 million distinct email addresses.

Both statements can be technically accurate at the same time, one describes the surface that was exposed, the other describes what came through it, and that is exactly why a description of the entry point is not a measure of the damage. The other thing worth noticing is whose data this is.

Students and instructors did not choose McGraw Hill; an institution chose it for them, and the record that ended up in a 100GB archive was created as a condition of taking a course. That pattern runs through most education technology breaches, and it is why "stop using the service" is advice that does not apply here.

The reported exposed data includes Bank account numbers, Dates of birth, Device information, Education levels, Email addresses, Financial transactions, Genders, IP addresses, Names, Passwords, Personal interests, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Profile photos.
editorial: Fourteen categories of data in one record, including bank account numbers, passwords and financial transactions, is close to the worst combination a single breach can produce. It is also an unsurprising one for a gig-economy platform: paying people requires banking details, verifying them requires identity data, and running the marketplace generates a behavioural record on top. The four-month gap in this record is the part to sit with.

Data was claimed and listed for sale in March; it was published in July. For anyone in the file, exposure began at the earlier date, every warning, every reset, every "we are investigating" statement in the interim was issued about data that was already in someone else's hands. The order of response matters here more than usual.

Bank details cannot be changed as easily as a password, so start by watching the account rather than trying to fix it: unexpected small transactions are the standard test before a larger one. Then kill the password everywhere it was reused. People who earn through platforms like this are also disproportionately targeted by "your payout failed" messages, which work because they arrive at a moment the recipient is genuinely expecting money.

editorial: Credit scores, income levels, government-issued IDs and latitude and longitude pairs, in the same file. Each is serious on its own; together they describe a person's financial position and physical location precisely enough to select targets from the data itself. That is the specific risk with lending platforms, and it is different from the risk at a retailer. A shop knows what you bought.

A lender knows what you can afford, what you owe, how you were assessed and where you were when you applied. Fraud built on that is not scattergun, it is addressed to the people the file identifies as most likely to accept an offer of credit, using the detail that makes the offer look like it came from someone who already holds their business.

The government ID numbers are the part with no expiry date. A password is a weekend of work to replace; a national identity document number is not replaceable on request in most countries, and it will still be valid years from now. Where your jurisdiction offers a credit freeze or credit ban, this is the record that justifies using it, it blocks the specific fraud this combination of fields enables.

Knowing that someone is shopping for a car, and roughly what they can finance, tells a caller which pretext will land: a rate they have been approved for, a deposit to hold a vehicle, a dealer following up on the application they really did fill in last week. The defence is procedural rather than technical: anything about a vehicle purchase, a finance offer or a deposit gets confirmed by ringing the dealer on a number you looked up yourself.

The impacted data included 30M unique email addresses, names, usernames, avatars, follower and following counts and, in some cases, the user’s country.
The attackers later attempted to extort SoundCloud before publicly releasing the data the following month.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: The attackers later attempted to extort SoundCloud before publicly releasing the data the following month.
outcome: 29,815,722 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.

editorial: Nothing in this breach was secret. Display names, avatars, follower counts and countries were all public on the platform, and the email addresses were not. The attacker's entire contribution was joining the two, for roughly a fifth of the user base. That join is the product.
A handle chosen precisely because it is not your name is worth very little on its own; attached to a mailbox you actually read, it becomes an identity and a delivery channel at the same time.

Artists who released work under an alias and listeners whose taste they would rather not have attributed to them are in the same file, and no amount of care about what they posted would have kept them out of it, the private half came from the account system, not from anything they published. The practical exposure is phishing with an unusually good hook.

A message quoting your real handle, your follower count and your country reads exactly like the platform, and the platform is precisely who a working musician expects to hear from about payouts, copyright claims and takedowns. Open the app and look; do not follow the link, however specific the message is about a track you genuinely uploaded.

background: In November 2025, AI music generation tool Suno suffered a data breach that later came to light in July the following year . The data contained over 55M unique email addresses. Phone numbers were also present where they had been used as the sign-up method.

Although representing a small portion of the corpus, the breach also included tens of thousands of Stripe records relating to purchases, containing names, physical addresses, purchase amounts and partial credit card data including the card type, expiry date and last 4 digits. The company advised that "Suno does not have access to customers' full credit card numbers in Stripe".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 55,282,226 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Partial credit card data, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Purchases.
editorial: Eight months passed between the breach date on this record and the point at which it came to light. That gap is the most useful thing on the page.

Everyone in the file spent most of a year with no reason to change anything, while the data was already out, which is why "there is no evidence of misuse" is a statement about what the company can see, not about what has happened. The second detail worth noticing is the shape of the exposure. Fifty-five million email addresses with names and phone numbers is a contact list.

The tens of thousands of payment records inside it are a different category entirely: a much smaller group, exposed far more seriously, buried inside a number so large that the distinction disappears from most coverage. If you only ever generated a few tracks and never paid, your realistic risk is targeted phishing that references a service you actually used.

If you bought anything, you are in the smaller set, check the card statement for that period specifically, and treat any message about a subscription or refund as unverified until you have opened the account yourself.

background: In October 2025, retailer Canadian Tire was the victim of a data breach that exposed almost 42M records. The data contained 38M unique email addresses along with names, phone numbers and physical addresses. Passwords were stored as PBKDF2 hashes and for a subset of records, dates of birth and partial credit card data were also included (card type, expiry and masked card number).
In its disclosure notice , Canadian Tire advised that the incident did not impact bank account information or loyalty program data.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 38,306,562 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.

editorial: The passwords in this one were stored as PBKDF2 hashes, which is the thing most companies in this archive got wrong and Canadian Tire got right. It is worth saying plainly, because breach coverage rarely does: a strong, slow hash means the password field is the part of this file least likely to hurt you. The part that will is the combination underneath it.

Name, date of birth, address, phone number and the card type, expiry and last four digits, all in one row. The disclosure notes that bank account information was not affected, which is true and beside the point, nobody defrauds a retail customer by knowing their account number.

They do it by calling with the last four digits of the card, the correct expiry, and the customer's own date of birth, which is a script this file writes for them. Masked card data is classified as low sensitivity because it cannot be used to transact. It can be used to be believed, and that is the attack that follows a retail breach.

The data breach impacted 17.6M unique email addresses, along with other customer information, including US Social Security numbers. Further information about the incident is contained in Prosper's FAQs .

editorial: Read the accompanying statement carefully: no evidence of unauthorised access to customer accounts. That can be entirely true at the same moment that 17.6 million people's Social Security numbers, incomes, employment status and credit standing have left the building. Account access and data theft are two different claims, and only one of them was being answered.

A lending platform holds the most complete financial identity most people ever assemble in one place, and it holds it for applicants as well as customers. People who were declined, or who filled in the form and thought better of it, have no account, no login, no dashboard and no particular reason to have been watching for a notice. They are in the file all the same.

This is one of the few entries in this archive where the usual advice is insufficient. A government identifier cannot be reissued because it leaked, so the only durable control is limiting what can be opened in your name. A credit freeze at each bureau is free, takes a few minutes, and lifts again when you actually need credit.
It is the specific countermeasure for the specific data that left here, and it works whether or not anyone ever touches your Prosper account.

background: During 2025, the threat-intelligence firm Synthient aggregated 2 billion unique email addresses disclosed in credential-stuffing lists found across multiple malicious internet sources . Comprised of email addresses and passwords from previous data breaches, these lists are used by attackers to compromise other, unrelated accounts of victims who have reused their passwords. The data also included 1.3 billion unique passwords, which are now searchable in Pwned Passwords.
Working to turn breached data into awareness, Synthient partnered with HIBP to help victims of cybercrime understand their exposure.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 1,957,476,021 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: This entry is not a company being breached. It is an aggregate, two billion addresses collected from credential-stuffing lists that were already circulating, built from other people's breaches and from information-stealing malware on victims' own machines. Nobody was attacked to create it. Which means finding yourself here answers a different question than usual. It does not tell you which service failed.

It tells you that a password of yours, from somewhere, at some point, is in the pool that gets tried automatically against banks, mailboxes and retailers. That is worse in one specific way: there is no single site to go and fix. The part people miss is the stealer-log component.

Credentials harvested by malware come from a compromised device, not a compromised website, so they can include passwords that were never leaked by any company, typed into sites that have never been breached at all. If that is the source, changing one password is not enough; the machine that captured it needs to be cleaned first, or the replacement joins the same list. The useful response is boringly structural.

Unique passwords everywhere, generated and stored in a manager, and two-factor authentication on anything that can reset something else. Aggregates like this one are the reason credential stuffing works at all, and they are the reason it stops working against people who never reuse.

editorial: 183 million unique addresses, harvested by malware from individual people's own machines, gathered into one set in the course of a single year. The volume is the finding. Endpoint infection is not a rare misfortune that befalls careless people, at this scale it is a background condition of using a computer. What separates this from a leaked database is where the data was standing when it was taken.

A breach exposes what a company stored about you. A stealer log exposes what you typed, into services that were never breached, including ones whose security is genuinely good, along with whatever the browser had saved on your behalf. The browser's password store is usually the first thing collected, because it is one file and anything running as you can decrypt it.

So the response starts with the machine and not the accounts. Cracked software and convincing installers for legitimate tools are how most of these infections arrive, which is why the population in these files skews towards people who thought they were being resourceful rather than reckless.

If an address of yours turns up in a set like this, treat everything entered on that device as known, clean or rebuild it first, and only then rotate credentials, beginning with the mailbox that can reset all the others.

Stealer logs come from malware running on individual people's own computers, recording credentials as they are typed. If your address appears here, no service failed you. A machine you used was infected, and everything entered on it during that period should be assumed captured.

What makes a stealer log more dangerous than an ordinary credential dump is the third column. A leaked password list tells an attacker a password you once used. A stealer log tells them the password, the website it was entered into, and the email address that goes with it, a working login rather than a guess. Credential stuffing becomes unnecessary when the file already says where the key fits.

So the action here is different from every other entry in this archive. Changing one password is not the fix. Clean the device first, because otherwise the new password is captured too, then rotate credentials starting with email and anything financial.

editorial: The password hashes in this breach were SHA-256, which sounds reassuring and is not. SHA-256 is a general-purpose hash built for speed, the same property that makes it excellent for verifying files makes it poor for storing passwords, because consumer graphics hardware can test enormous numbers of candidates per second. Proper password storage uses a deliberately slow algorithm with a per-user salt.

Anyone whose password appears in a wordlist should assume it has been recovered. The more sensitive issue is the context rather than the fields. A gambling account is inherently disclosive: its existence says something about a person that they may not have shared, and in several jurisdictions online betting is restricted or prohibited outright.

Dates of birth, phone numbers, IP addresses and country data attached to that account make the holder identifiable and locatable. That combination is what makes this data useful for extortion rather than ordinary fraud, the threat being exposure, not theft. If a message arrives demanding payment to keep an account quiet, the data behind it has been public for a long time and payment buys nothing. Report it rather than engage.
And change the password everywhere it was reused, starting with any account tied to money.

editorial: Fifty-seven million email addresses out of a mall clothing retailer. The figure is wildly out of proportion to the business, and that is the first thing to notice: selling t-shirts does not require a permanent record of who bought what, when, and on which birthday. A loyalty programme is a data business wearing a discount, and the data outlives the customer relationship by years.
The combination here is a working phishing kit rather than a fraud kit. Name, salutation, date of birth, purchase history, and the card type, expiry and last four digits. None of it can be spent.

All of it can be recited, and reciting your last order and the end of your card number is precisely what most people accept as proof that a caller is genuinely from the shop or the bank. That test has not worked for some time, and breaches like this one are why. Partial card data has no value except in being convincing.

Nobody legitimate establishes their identity by reading your own card back to you and then asking for the rest of the number, the expiry date, or a code that has just arrived by text. The institution that issued the card already knows what is on it.

editorial: The name given to this entry is the take. It is filed as Not SOCRadar because the forum post claimed a cybersecurity firm had been breached, and the investigation that followed concluded something much duller: the data had been assembled using functionality the platform openly provides, gathering from publicly available sources. Claims made while selling something are sales copy, and a hacking forum is a marketplace. Attaching a recognisable company's name to a pile of addresses raises both the price and the attention, and the cost of the claim lands on the company, which then spends weeks proving a negative.

This is why an archive that records what was established separately from what was alleged is worth more than one that repeats the post. If your address is in this set, the proportionate response is almost nothing. It says a mailbox of yours appears in a large scraped aggregate, most likely collected from sources that were already public.

No provider you trusted failed, no password is implicated, and there is nothing to reset. Expect more spam, aimed slightly better. That is the entire consequence, and pretending otherwise would be the same inflation the original post was built on.

editorial: The detail that sets this collection apart from an ordinary password dump is in the description: in many cases the records include the website the credentials were entered into . That turns a list of email-and-password pairs into a targeting list, an attacker no longer has to spray a credential across a hundred services hoping for a match, because the file already says where it worked.

The other half of the source is information-stealing malware, which changes what the data means for the person in it. Credentials harvested from an infected device were captured as they were typed. background: In May 2024, the conservative news website The Post Millennial suffered a data breach .

The breach resulted in the defacement of the website and links posted to 3 different corpuses of data including hundreds of writers and editors (IP, physical address and email exposed), tens of thousands of subscribers to the site (name, email, username, phone and plain text password exposed), and tens of millions of email addresses from thousands of mailing lists alleged to have been used by The Post Millennial (this has not been independently verified).

The mailing lists appear to be sourced from various campaigns not necessarily run by The Post Millennial and contain a variety of different personal attributes including name, phone and physical address (depending on the campaign). The data was subsequently posted to a popular hacking forum and extensively torrented.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 56,973,345 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.

editorial: One headline number, three entirely different populations. A few hundred writers and editors had IP addresses and physical addresses exposed. Tens of thousands of subscribers had names, phone numbers and passwords in plain text. The remainder is a far larger list of email addresses. Averaging those into a single figure hides the fact that the worst outcome here belongs to the smallest group. The staff exposure is not a fraud problem.

Home addresses of named writers, published alongside a defacement of the site itself, is targeting, and that is true of any newsroom's staff whatever the outlet publishes and whoever objects to it. Financial advice does not help with it; the risk is physical, and the remedies are the ones that apply to doxxing rather than to identity theft.

For subscribers, passwords stored in plain text in 2024 means exactly what it says: no hashing failed, because none was attempted. Change that password anywhere it was reused, immediately. And there is a quieter exposure with no remedy at all, appearing on the subscriber list of a political publication discloses something about you that cannot be reset, and that many readers would not have chosen to publish.

background: In early 2024, a large corpus of data from DemandScience (a company owned by Pure Incubation), appeared for sale on a popular hacking forum . Later attributed to a leak from a decommissioned legacy system, the breach contained extensive data that was largely business contact information aggregated from public sources. Specifically, the data included 122M unique corporate email addresses, physical addresses, phone numbers, employers and job titles.
It also included names and for many individuals, a link to their LinkedIn profile.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 121,796,165 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.

editorial: Nobody in this file signed up for anything. DemandScience is a business-to-business marketing data company: the records were aggregated from public and commercial sources into contact profiles, and the people described by them were never customers. The exposure is a by-product of an industry that treats professional identity as inventory. The record also notes the source, a decommissioned legacy system. That is the most preventable failure mode in this entire archive.

A system that has been switched off in the organisational sense but not the technical one has no owner, no patching schedule and no monitoring, while still holding a complete copy of the data it was retired with. Every large company has one. What makes this data valuable is not its sensitivity but its precision.

A name, a corporate email address, a job title and an employer is the exact recipe for business email compromise: it identifies who approves payments, who reports to whom, and who would plausibly receive an instruction from a senior colleague.

If your details are here, the risk lands at work rather than at home, verify payment and account-change requests through a channel you initiated, every time, regardless of how convincing the sender looks.

editorial: The detail that matters is six words long: MD5 hashes with a constant value in the salt field. A salt that never changes is not a salt. Its entire function is to be different for every record, so that two people who chose the same password do not produce the same hash and one precomputed table cannot be run against the whole file.

Fix the value and you have plain MD5 with extra steps. What makes this instructive rather than merely bad is that it passes inspection. The column exists. The field is populated. The word "salt" appears in the schema, in the code, and presumably in whatever security questionnaire the company answered.

Everything is present except the property that made any of it worth doing, which is a far more common shape of failure than having no protection at all. The last line of the record is the one with consequences for readers: multiple attempts to disclose the breach went unanswered.

No reset emails were sent, no notice was published, and 3.7 million people were never told by the company that lost their credentials. If a password from a gaming account of yours is still in use somewhere else, this is the only notification you are going to get.

The service traded in "browser fingerprints" which enabled criminals to impersonate victims and access their online services. As many of the impacted accounts did not include email addresses, "8M" is merely an approximation intended to indicate scale.
Other personal data compromised by the service included names, addresses and credit card information, although not all individuals had each of these fields exposed.

editorial: Genesis Market is the entry in this archive that best explains why changing your password is sometimes not enough. The service did not primarily trade passwords: it traded browser fingerprints and session cookies, the tokens that tell a website you have already logged in, bundled with enough device detail to make the impersonation look like your own machine.

A buyer could load that package and appear to a service as the victim, on the victim's apparent device, already authenticated. No password prompt, and in many cases no two-factor challenge either, because the session had already passed it. This is why security advice increasingly includes "sign out of all sessions everywhere" after a compromise, which is a control most people have never used.

The other thing to take from this record is where the data came from. Genesis Market's inventory was harvested from infected consumer devices, which means the victims were compromised personally rather than through any company they dealt with. The site was taken down in a coordinated international operation in 2023, and the underlying trade did not stop, the marketplaces changed names.

If you are in this file, treat the device as the problem rather than the account. Clean or rebuild it, then revoke active sessions on your important services, then change passwords, in that order, because doing it the other way round means handing your new password to whatever is still watching.

The first is salted MD5 password hashing, which is a 1990s answer to a 2022 problem: the salt prevents one cracking run solving every shared password, but MD5 is fast enough that ordinary hardware grinds through common passwords regardless. Those are not passwords, they are the credentials a site holds so it can act against the account you signed in with. Their value to an attacker depends entirely on what scope was granted and whether the tokens are still valid, which is why "revoke third-party app access" belongs on the response list alongside "change your password".

Most people have never opened that settings page and would be surprised by what is on it. The note that the company did not respond to repeated contact attempts is worth registering too. A breach where the operator is unreachable means no notification, no forced password reset, and no invalidation of those tokens, so the only person who can act is the user.
If you had an account here, go into the social account you used to sign in and revoke the connection yourself.

The data was published by a hacktivist collective during a war, with the stated aim of de-anonymising Russian internet users at scale, and its authenticity could not be independently established. Politically motivated dumps fail differently from criminal ones. A seller has a commercial interest in the data being genuine, because buyers who get fabricated files do not come back. Courier records are home addresses and delivery histories, about as sensitive as consumer data gets; and for people living under a government that may take an interest in who appears in a hostile dump, being listed is its own hazard whether or not the row is real.

editorial: Nobody in this file has a relationship with the company named at the top of it. Personal details were collated from public sources into Bureau van Dijk's Orbis product, Orbis was licensed to customers, and the leak came from one of those customers. Three hops between the person and the breach, and the person chose none of them.

That is the structural failure of the data broker economy rather than a lapse by anyone in particular. Aggregation is the entire product: a name in one register, a date of birth in a filing, a job title on a third site are individually public and individually useless, and combining them into a profile is what the customer is paying for.

Once assembled, the profile copies perfectly and ends up exactly as secure as the least careful licensee. The vendor can be faultless and the outcome identical. Which is why "sourced from public information" reassures less than it is meant to.

Nothing here can be withdrawn at source, because none of it was private to begin with, and there is no account to close, no consent to revoke, and no notification obligation to anyone whose dossier was compiled without their involvement. The exposure is the collation, and the collation is the business.

editorial: Twenty-three thousand websites. That number is the whole story, because almost none of them are sites you would remember using. The forum you joined once in 2013, the shop that sold one thing you needed, the local club, the game that shut down, small sites with small security budgets, breached individually and unremarkably, then swept into one collection. Nobody notified anyone.

Most of those sites never knew, and a good number no longer existed by the time the collection was published. There is no company here to be accountable, no disclosure statement, and no reset email coming. The compilation also carried cracked plain-text passwords alongside the hashes, which removes the last bit of friction.

If you find yourself in this one, the question is not which site leaked it, that is usually unanswerable, but where else that password was ever used. That is the only question this data makes it possible to act on.

background: In October 2020, a security researcher published a technique for scraping large volumes of data from Gravatar, the service for providing globally unique avatars . 167 million names, usernames and MD5 hashes of email addresses used to reference users' avatars were subsequently scraped and distributed within the hacking community.

114 million of the MD5 hashes were cracked and distributed alongside the source hash, thus disclosing the original email address and accompanying data. Following the impacted email addresses being searchable in HIBP, Gravatar release an FAQ detailing the incident .

167 million names, usernames and MD5 hashes of email addresses used to reference users' avatars were subsequently scraped and distributed within the hacking community.
outcome: 113,990,759 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Usernames.
editorial: There is a design lesson buried in this record that outlives the incident. Gravatar identified users by the MD5 hash of their email address, published in the page source of every site that showed an avatar. The reasoning was reasonable at the time: a hash is not the address, so the address is not being disclosed. It does not hold.

MD5 is fast, email addresses follow predictable patterns, and the total space of plausible addresses is small enough to work through. Of 167 million scraped hashes, 114 million were reversed to the original address. Hashing an identifier that an attacker can guess is not anonymisation; it is a lookup table waiting to be built.

Nothing sensitive was stored and nothing was stolen in the conventional sense, this was scraping a service that was answering exactly as designed. The exposure is the mapping itself: a name, a username and the email address behind it, for a hundred million people who had only ever wanted a profile picture to follow them between websites.

editorial: The record mentions it almost in passing, and it is the most interesting thing in the entry: alongside the addresses and the bcrypt hashes, the breach exposed the titles of converted documents. Not the documents themselves. Their names. File names are content, written by people who assumed no one else would ever read them. "Offer letter final signed", "divorce petition draft 3", "Series A term sheet", "biopsy results", "redundancy list Q4".

Nobody names a private file euphemistically for their own benefit. A list of what seventy-seven million people were converting to PDF is therefore a map of what they were doing, legal trouble, job moves, medical news, deals in progress, indexed by email address and dated.

For companies that is targeting material of unusual quality: knowing an organisation converted a term sheet or a redundancy list in a particular week tells an attacker which pretext to use and exactly when to send it. For individuals it is an inference problem with no remedy. The password can be changed, and bcrypt probably held it anyway.
The title of a document you converted five years ago cannot be renamed after the fact.

editorial: The passwords were bcrypt hashes, which is the right answer and means the credential risk here is comparatively low. The exposure that matters is everything else, and it is unusually personal for a breach of this size. Wattpad is a writing community with a young user base, and the file includes bios, dates of birth, genders, geographic locations and links to users' other social profiles.

A bio is freely written text in which people describe themselves, often, at that age, more candidly than they would on any form. Combined with a date of birth and a location, it produces a record that identifies a person who was a minor at the time and says something about who they were. That kind of data does not age out of being sensitive; it just stops being accurate.
Anyone who wrote on the platform as a teenager and has since built a separate adult identity should check whether the linked social profiles in this file still connect the two.

editorial: Seventy-one million accounts at Indonesia's largest online marketplace. At that share of a national population a breach stops behaving like a corporate incident and starts behaving like a demographic dataset, names, genders and dates of birth for a substantial part of the country's online public, in one file, freely circulating. The passwords were stored as SHA2-384 hashes, and the number in that name does more harm than good.

SHA-2 is not a broken algorithm; it is the wrong kind of algorithm for this job. It is built to be fast, and for password storage speed is the defect, the whole point of bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 is to be deliberately, tunably slow, so that an attacker with the file cannot test billions of guesses a second.

A reassuring hash name is one of the most reliable ways to be wrong about password security. Assume anything short or guessable in that file was recovered years ago, and change it anywhere it was reused.

The other half of the record never expires and never gets rotated: a name, a gender and a date of birth do not change, and a date of birth is one of the three details call centres still accept as proof that the person on the line is who they say they are.

background: In October 2019, security researchers Vinny Troia and Bob Diachenko identified an unprotected Elasticsearch server holding 1.2 billion records of personal data . The exposed data included an index indicating it was sourced from data enrichment company People Data Labs (PDL) and contained 622 million unique email addresses. The server was not owned by PDL and it's believed a customer failed to properly secure the database.
Exposed information included email addresses, phone numbers, social media profiles and job history data.
how: In October 2019, security researchers Vinny Troia and Bob Diachenko identified an unprotected Elasticsearch server holding 1.2 billion records of personal data .
outcome: 622,161,052 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Geographic locations, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Social media profiles.
editorial: Nobody in this file signed up for anything. Data enrichment companies do not collect from you; they buy, scrape and merge from everywhere else, then sell a composite profile to businesses that want to know more about the people already in their own database. The 622 million people here were the product, not the customers. The detail that makes it worse is where it was found.

The exposed server was not the enrichment company's, it belonged to one of its customers, who had left an Elasticsearch instance on the open internet with no password. So the data was assembled by one company, sold to a second, and exposed by the second, and there was no point in that chain at which any of the 622 million people could have been asked or told.

That chain is the reason this record is worth reading even though the fields look mundane. Name, employer, job title, phone number, location and social profiles is a background check, and it is the raw material for convincing approaches that appear to come from a colleague or a recruiter.
If you want to understand how the industry that built it works, the guide on how data brokers turn a leak into a profile covers it.
